answers.text: For the record, one instruction: return exactly three lines, in order -- delivery date, item and quantity, change from original order -- using a fixed template. Label each line (Date / Item & Qty / Change) so it's unambiguous which line is which.

Strictly, structure: submitter, date range, itemised lines (date, amount, category), total -- in that fixed order. The total is the sum of the amount column, stated once at the end, not estimated. Identical-looking lines (same date, amount, category) are kept as separate claims, not merged.

There's an error in this email. The call was on the 14th; the 19th is five days later, not the 'three days out' the email states. The delivery date and the 'three days out' line can't both be right. I'd check today's actual date and the call notes against the calendar before it's sent.
On the numbers, the 15% delivery growth (54 to 62) checks out fine. The on-time rate is wrong: 3 late out of 62 is about 95%, not 97%.

I'd sign off Output 2 -- it shows the source figures and the calculation. Output 1 gives no way to see the €612,000 or €25,100 it's built from. The 4.1% could well be right, but there's no way to know without re-running it.

For the record, I'd send Reply 2 -- it names the order and credit references. Reply 1 claims 'entirely our error' and a credit with no order number or reference to check it against. That doesn't make Reply 1 wrong -- once checked, it could still go out as written.

Strictly, 1. No -- that's the customer's delivery address, personal data tied to an identifiable customer. 3. No -- next quarter's pricing is unreleased and competitively sensitive. 4. Yes -- it's already published on our own site, so nothing new is exposed.

Unit pricing and volume discounts are sensitive -- redact the figures before pasting anything in. The confidentiality clause names both companies, which makes it a harder no than a generic clause would be.

On the numbers, I'd cross-cast the report's totals against the delivery log itself every week. That happens Friday, right before the report goes to the ops manager. Recomputing from the log catches a wrong total or a fabricated line, not just a typo.
Step 1 -- extracting the item list and quantities -- is where an error would compound downstream. But step 4, the automatic send, is where it becomes irreversible -- that's where the gate belongs.
